title: Must We Suffer Emotional Pain?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore emotional pain: its definition (also called psychological or psychic pain), the Cartesian mind-body split in Western medicine, Edwin Schneidman's "psychache" concept, and the theory that emotional pain evolved from the physical pain system to protect social bonds. They cover Ethan Cross's fMRI study finding that emotional pain activates the same brain regions as physical heat pain, the vagus nerve and chest/abdomen sensations, effects of acetaminophen-type painkillers on emotional blunting, the lack of a validated mental pain scale, links to heartbreak, depression, eating disorders, borderline personality disorder, non-suicidal self-injury, rejection sensitive dysphoria, and suicide. They end with treatments (CBT, DBT, acceptance and commitment therapy, and Mark Rygo's medication-first view), and a listener phone call from John Hodgman about the origin of the word "pooh"/"peu" and "stinks".

segments.title: Opening and history of mind-body split
segments.summary: The hosts introduce emotional pain as a topic that Western medicine has long overlooked, define it, and trace the mind-body dualism back to Descartes in the seventeenth century. They mention Freud, Edwin Schneidman's concept of psychache, and a consensus definition of emotional pain as self-disappointment.

segments.title: Break and jokes
segments.summary: A brief break; the hosts discuss joking about emotional pain and a listener's offended reaction to a Midwest joke.

segments.title: Social pain and evolutionary origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss social pain as tied to social interactions such as rejection, and the theory that emotional pain evolved from the physical pain system because social bonds mattered for survival.

segments.title: Brain imaging of emotional pain
segments.summary: Studies using fMRI show emotional pain activates the same brain regions as physical pain. Ethan Cross's study at the University of Michigan used recently dumped participants and a painful heat comparison, finding similar activation in sensory and affective regions.

segments.title: Physical symptoms and the vagus nerve
segments.summary: The hosts describe physical sensations of emotional distress, citing research linking the anterior cingulate cortex and the vagus nerve to chest and abdominal discomfort. They discuss how emotional pain persists into adulthood.

segments.title: Coping, nature walks, and painkiller effects
segments.summary: The hosts compare acute physical pain with emotional pain, note that emotional pain signals a need for self-care, and mention that walking outdoors helps. They then discuss how acetaminophen-type painkillers may blunt emotional responses and empathy.

segments.title: Measuring emotional pain and related conditions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the lack of a validated mental pain scale, a British Medical Journal review of ten scales, and heartbreak as a form of drug withdrawal-like experience with stress hormones and possible takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

segments.title: Depression, eating disorders, and borderline personality disorder
segments.summary: Emotional pain is distinguished from depression though they correlate. Eating disorders are described as coping with emotional pain. Borderline personality disorder is discussed as a source of chronic, intense pain tied to abandonment fears.

segments.title: Self-injury, rejection sensitive dysphoria, suicide, and treatments
segments.summary: The hosts discuss non-suicidal self-injury, rejection sensitive dysphoria, suicidal ideation linked to psychological pain, and treatments including CBT, DBT, ACT, and Mark Rygo's medication-first view. They close with a listener phone call from John Hodgman about the origin of the word 'peu' and a ponytail anecdote.
